lesson.title: Hallucinogens: Rewiring Perception at the Receptor Level
lesson.summary: Hallucinogens alter perception and thought by acting on serotonin and cannabinoid receptors, disrupting the brain's normal filtering of sensory and cognitive information.
lesson.body:
Hallucinogens are psychoactive drugs that alter perception, mood, and thought in ways that can include seeing, hearing, or feeling things that are not really there, along with a distorted sense of time, space, or self. Unlike stimulants and depressants, which mainly turn overall nervous system activity up or down, hallucinogens work by disrupting the normal patterns of communication within specific brain circuits, especially ones involved in filtering and interpreting sensory information.

Classic hallucinogens such as LSD and psilocybin, the active compound in certain mushrooms, are agonists at a specific subtype of serotonin receptor called 5 HT2A. Serotonin normally activates this receptor as part of everyday mood and cognitive regulation, but LSD and psilocybin bind it more persistently and in a somewhat different pattern than serotonin does, which appears to disrupt the usual filtering that keeps unrelated sensory and cognitive information from bleeding into one another. That disrupted filtering is one leading explanation for why users report unusual sensory blending and shifts in the sense of self.

This mechanism is worth contrasting with the agonists covered earlier in this unit. Morphine's agonism at opioid receptors produces a fairly predictable, dose dependent effect: more drug generally means more pain relief and sedation. Hallucinogen agonism at serotonin receptors is far less linear, because the 5 HT2A receptor sits inside a dense, highly interconnected cortical network, so a relatively small chemical event can cascade into a large and unpredictable shift in conscious experience.

THC, the main psychoactive compound in marijuana, works through a related but distinct system. It is an agonist at cannabinoid receptors, mainly the CB1 subtype, which are normally activated by the brain's own endocannabinoid chemicals, most notably a molecule called anandamide. THC's effects, including altered time perception, changes in appetite, and at higher doses mild hallucinatory experiences, come from activating this cannabinoid system more strongly and for longer than the body's own signaling typically would.

Classic hallucinogens are also unusual compared with most other drugs in this unit because they do not reliably produce the compulsive craving or physical withdrawal associated with stimulants, depressants, or opioids. They do produce a rapid, short lived tolerance with repeated daily use, sometimes called tachyphylaxis, in which the same dose taken again the next day produces a much weaker effect, but that tolerance fades quickly once use stops, and there is little evidence of the kind of receptor downregulation driven physical dependence described in later chapters.

What unites hallucinogens as a category is not a shared neurotransmitter system but a shared outcome: each one, through its own specific receptor mechanism, pushes perception and thought outside their normal operating range rather than simply amplifying or dampening the nervous system's overall activity level the way stimulants and depressants do.
